title: What it doesn't show
hook: many early studies were small, and the effects are often modest

segments.voice: Yesterday: what meditation research shows, forty-seven trials, modest help for anxiety, depression and pain. Your line was moderate, and real. How did you feel after sitting? Day three hundred six.

Picture a magazine cover. A glowing brain, lit up in orange and blue, and a person sitting cross-legged in front of a sunrise. The headline: meditation rebuilds your brain in eight weeks. You've probably seen something like it, maybe more than once. It's a beautiful picture. And it's one reason a group of scientists who study meditation, people who believe it's worth studying, wrote a paper warning everyone to calm down. Yesterday was what the research shows. Today is the other half, just as important. Today: what it doesn't show.
screen: `A GLOWING BRAIN ON A COVER.` → `REBUILDS YOUR BRAIN IN EIGHT WEEKS.` → `SCIENTISTS SAY CALM DOWN.`

segments.voice: In 2018 fifteen researchers, led by Nicholas Van Dam, published a paper called Mind the Hype, in the journal Perspectives on Psychological Science. Most of them had spent their careers on meditation research. Here is what they said, in plain terms. First, nobody agrees what the word mindfulness means. It can mean a trait, a state, a practice, a program or a whole tradition, so two studies of mindfulness may not be measuring the same thing. Second, many studies, especially the early ones, were small. Remember the coins: a study of twenty or thirty people can find a big effect just by chance. Third, many had weak comparisons, a waitlist that did nothing instead of an active group. Fourth, brain scan studies are especially tempting to over-read. A region looks different in a small group of meditators; that doesn't mean you'll grow a new brain by Friday. There's also a quieter problem across science: studies that find nothing are less likely to get published, so the shelf of published papers can look rosier than reality. And last, the effects that do hold up are often modest, and they're usually no bigger than other good options, like exercise or therapy. None of this says meditation is useless. Yesterday's review stands. It says the honest claims are smaller than the magazine covers. And that matters for a person, not only for scientists. If you expect magic, you'll either quit when it doesn't come or blame yourself. If you expect something modest and real, you can keep going. No magic. Just practice.
screen: `MIND THE HYPE, 2018.` · `NO AGREED MEANING OF MINDFULNESS.` · `SMALL STUDIES, WEAK COMPARISONS.` · `BRAIN SCANS ARE EASY TO OVER-READ.` · then, large: `NO MAGIC.`

segments.voice: Notice any hope you've been carrying about practice. That it will fix your sleep, or your temper, or make you a calmer person by spring. Name it kindly. Now set it down beside you, like a bag you don't need to carry into the room. Sit without it. Just breath, just attention, just these two minutes, asking nothing of them. The bell holds the time.
What it doesn't show. Many early studies were small, comparisons weak, and effects modest: meditation is real practice, not magic. Today's word.
Your line: no magic. Keep your expectations honest today. If you meet a big claim about any practice, ask how big the study was. Day three hundred six.

howItsDone: Researchers now call for larger trials, active control groups, clear definitions of mindfulness and cautious reporting, and many teachers present meditation's benefits as modest.

fork.setup: you started meditating expecting to be transformed in a month. it hasn't happened. what does today's lesson suggest?
options: expect something modest and real, and keep going.
fork.reveal: honest expectations keep you practicing: the effects that hold up are real but usually modest.

trapdoor: what you thought: research shows meditation transforms your brain.
what it means: many studies were small, comparisons weak, and effects modest.
what a scholar hears: Van Dam et al. (2018) on definitional confusion, underpowered samples, weak controls and publication bias.

notes: Van Dam et al. (2018): fifteen authors; confirm author count and journal details.
